# Automation Error Type and Methods of Communicating Automation Reliability Affect Trust and Performance: An Empirical Study in the Cyber Domain

Jing Chen , Member, IEEE, Scott Mishler, and Bin Hu, Member, IEEE

**Abstract—Antiphishing aid systems, among other automated systems, are not perfectly reliable. Automated systems can make errors, thereby resulting in false alarms or misses. An automated system’s capabilities need to be communicated to the users to maintain proper user trust. System capabilities can be learned through an explicit description or from experience. Using a phishing-detection system as a testbed in this article, we systematically varied automation error type and the method of communicating system reliability in a factorial design and measured their effects on human performance and trust in the automation. Participants were asked to classify emails as legitimate or phishing with assistance from the phishing-detection system. The results from 510 participants suggest that learning through experience with feedback improved trust calibration for both objective and subjective trust measures in most conditions. Moreover, false alarms lowered trust more than misses for both unreliable and reliable systems, and false alarms turned out to be beneficial for proper trust calibration when using unreliable systems. Design implications of the results include using feedback whenever possible and choosing false alarms over misses for unreliable systems.**

**Index Terms—Cyberspace, decision making, decision support systems, human computer interaction, human factors.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

<sup>UTOMATED</sup> systems are prevalent in modern society, A with examples from intelligent transportation systems, smart manufacturing systems, smart homes, and various automated aids used in people’s lives. An automated aid system can make errors, such as false alarms and misses, which lead to imperfect system reliability. The reliability of an automated aid can be learned in two ways: A user can be told about it explicitly (i.e., description) or learn about it through using the system (i.e., experience). Our goal was to examine the effects of automation error type and the methods of communicating reliability on user performance and trust in automated systems using automated phishing detection systems as an example domain.

Phishing emails are often disguised as trustworthy emails and attempt to obtain sensitive information for malicious reasons [1], [2]. The human user is considered the weakest link in cybersecurity [3], [4], and thus, it is important to study how users make decisions as well as how automated tools support users decisions. In the case of phishing, common users are typically incapable of accurately distinguishing phishing emails or websites from legitimate emails or websites [5]. Antiphishing tools are a means of helping users detect phishing emails or websites [1], [6], [7]. However, similar to other types of automated aids, these tools are not perfect and can make errors resulting in false alarms (i.e., labeling a legitimate email as phishing) and misses (i.e., assuming a phishing email is legitimate).

## A. Trust in Automation

Human trust in automation has been widely studied because it affects how the human operator, or user, interacts with the automated system, which consequently influences the overall system performance [8]–[10]. We adopt the definition of trust by [11], “the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability” (p. 51). For an efficient human-automation system, neither too little trust (undertrust) nor too much trust (overtrust) is desirable [12], [13]. Human trust in the system should match the system capabilities or the ability to execute a specific course of action [14]. The human operator should calibrate her trust level to trust a system that is capable but distrust a system that is incapable (i.e., trust calibration) [9], [11], [15]. Among system capabilities, system reliability is one of the most important factors that affects trust, with higher reliability levels leading to higher trust levels [16], [17].

There are various automated systems in the cyber domain, although they are not often studied from this perspective. Examples include the antivirus software on one’s desktop, the spam filter in one’s email inbox, the autocomplete in search engines, and various antiphishing tools. Even though user trust has been discussed in the cyber domain [18]–[20], there have not been many empirical studies examining how trust affects human–automation interaction within the cyber context (see [12]). Research has shown that the effect of trust in automation may vary across different domains [21]. Given the prevalence of automated systems in cyberspace, human–automation interaction is essential for secure and efficient cyberspace. Motivated by this gap, the present study focused on the understudied trust in automation in the cyber domain.

## B. Methods of Communicating System Reliability

As discussed above, appropriate trust calibration (i.e., calibrating trust to match system capabilities) should depend on the system’s capabilities [9], [11], [15]. However, automation capabilities are not always obvious, and they need to be communicated to the human operator effectively. Thus, proper trust calibration relies on the human’s clear understanding of the system’s capabilities [11]. There are two general ways of communicating the system capabilities to the human operator [22]: through an explicit description of the capabilities (i.e., description) or through the operator’s use of the system and experiencing its successes and failures (i.e., experience).

In terms of automation reliability, researchers have typically used three types of measures, including accuracy (i.e., percentage of correct decisions), sensitivity (i.e., d’ from signal detection theory; SDT), and positive predictive value (i.e., percentage of correctly reporting target presence when the automation alarms) [23]–[25]. In this article, we used the measure of accuracy, which is essentially probabilistic knowledge about how the system performs, such as correctly indicating target present and target absent events [23], [25]. In [11], the basis of trust is described as information about automation in three areas (purpose, process, and performance). Purpose describes why automation is used, the process describes how automation operates, and performance describes what automation does or how well it performs. In the current context, both description and experience provide information in terms of the performance of the system.

Indeed, systematic discrepancies have been demonstrated between these two ways of gaining (probabilistic) knowledge in the human decision-making literature (i.e., the descriptionexperience gap) [26], [27]. For example, before deciding whether to make a bet, one wants to learn about the chance of winning. A person may be told about the probability of winning (i.e., description) or test it out by betting multiple times and learning the probability through corresponding outcomes (i.e., experience, with the outcomes as feedback). A typical finding is that when decisions are made based on description, small probabilities tend to be overweighed, whereas when decisions are made based on experience, small probabilities tend to be underweighted. This description-experience gap is a robust phenomenon that has been established through a substantial volume of literature (see [28] for a review). When investigating these two different methods of communicating system-reliability information in the applied area of human–automation interaction, critical differences can emerge, which researchers in this field need to consider [22], [29].

## C. Types of Automation Error

Trust in automation is affected not only by the reliability of the automation but also by the automation error types, false alarms and misses [30], [31]. With an automated aid, misses occur when the aid fails to detect and respond to a signal; false alarms occur when the aid falsely responds to no signal [23]. Misses and false alarms affect human performance in qualitatively different ways, with more serious damage being caused by false-alarm-prone automation than by missprone automation [26]. In addition, it has been found that false-alarm-prone automation reduces compliance (i.e., the operator’s reaction when the automation presents a warning), and missprone automation reduces reliance (i.e., the operator’s inaction when the automation remains silent) [24].

In the case of automated aids, there is usually a tradeoff between making false-alarm errors and allowing for misses [23]–[25]. In SDT, this tradeoff is captured as the response threshold or criterion of aid [23], [25]. For example, Yang et al. [6] developed an antiphishing aid called domain rank-based antiphishing warning (DRAW). This aid alerts users when the domain of a visited webpage has a traffic ranking lower than a certain threshold. DRAW is based on the rationale that phishing websites are typically visited infrequently and have low traffic. A threshold set at a low ranking will only lead to alerts of low traffic, infrequent websites. As a result, compared to a 10 000-ranking threshold, a 100 000-ranking threshold produces more misses (e.g., a phishing website with a traffic ranking of 99 999) but fewer false alarms (e.g., a legitimate website with a traffic ranking of 10 101). In other words, changing the threshold either increases misses and reduces false alarms or increases false alarms and reduces misses. Thus, there is a tradeoff between misses and false alarms. To determine an optimal threshold for antiphishing aids, it is critical to first study the role of error type in this specific context.

In summary, there have been few empirical studies about user trust in automation in the cyber domain. The current study is one of the first to empirically investigate how the methods of communicating system capability as well as the potential tradeoff between false alarms and misses affect users’ trust and performance when using automated aids in the cyber domain.

## II. CURRENT STUDY

The testbed used in this study was a phishing-detection system. Before the user classified an email as legitimate or phishing, this aid provided a recommendation. This automated system assists the user in the decision stage (i.e., functions as decision automation) [32]. The current study was built upon previous research [22] that first examined how methods of communicating system reliability information affected users’ trust and performance in a phishing context. It was previously found that describing the system reliability to participants at most led to an inflation of subjective trust reports, but communicating the system reliability through experience affected trust calibration for both subjective and objective trust measures [22]. In [22], the false alarm and miss rates were set to be equal and not manipulated. However, these two types of automation error could affect users’ interaction with the automated aid differently. The present study served the purposes of

1) verifying the previously revealed effects of the system reliability level (reliable versus unreliable) and the communication method (description versus experience),

2) investigating the role of error type (false alarms versus misses) in human–automation interaction in the cyber domain, and

3) exploring potential interactions between system reliability, the communication method, and error type.

For these purposes, we tested an unreliable system versus a reliable system (60% versus 90% correct recommendations), determined based on prior studies. For example, Rovira et al. [33] used 60% unreliable automation and 80% reliable automation in a stimulated command and control task. Moray et al. [34] used 70% as the unreliable automation level in contrast to 90% and 100% as the reliable levels in a fault management task and found a strong effect of reliability when it was below 90% but little difference when it was above 90%. To avoid the unrealistically perfect system of 100% and include a wide range of unreliable systems, Chen et al. [22] tested system reliability levels of 60%, 70%, 80%, and 90% and showed that the 90% reliable system yielded better performance and a higher user agreement rate with the system than the 60% reliable system. As a result, the current study used 60% reliability as unreliable and 90% reliability as reliable. For each reliability level, there were two error-type conditions: a false-alarm condition, with all automation errors being false alarms, and a miss condition, with all errors being misses.

System reliability was communicated to participants with a description method (with the exact percentage of correct automation recommendations described to the user: with versus without description conditions) or an experience method (with immediate feedback to help the user learn: with versus without feedback conditions). Although feedback and experience are different terms, feedback has been used as a manipulation of experience [22], [35], [36]. In the bet example we discussed in the Section I, for a person to learn the probability of a bet, the outcomes (a.k.a., feedback) of the bet are critical as part of the experience. Merely playing the bet without feedback will not serve the purpose of learning the probability. Similarly, the rationale is that experience is less about using the aid per se but more about learning the successes and failures of the aid, for which feedback is essential. Thus, we call the two conditions with feedback and without feedback, corresponding with more experience and less experience conditions.

As a result, the present study used a 2 (reliability: unreliable versus reliable) × 2 (error type: miss versus false alarm) × 2 (description: with versus without) × 2 (feedback: with versus without) design, with all factors being between-subjects. The measures of participants’ performance (response sensitivity and response bias in SDT and decision time) and trust (subjective and objective) were compared across the different conditions. The details of the conditions and measures are introduced in the Section III. The following main hypotheses were generated based on prior literature discussed above.

Hypothesis 1: Performance and trust measures were expected to increase as reliability increased (i.e., increased response sensitivity and both trust measures, reduced response bias and decision time) [16], [17], [22].

Hypothesis 2: Performance and trust measures were expected to improve (i.e., increased response sensitivity and both trust measures, reduced response bias and decision time) with feedback relative to without feedback [37], [38].

Hypothesis 3: Both the objective and subjective trust measures were expected to be higher in the 90% reliability condition than in the 60% reliability condition when feedback was provided but not when feedback was absent [22].

Hypothesis 4: Subjectively reported trust, not objectively measured trust, was expected to be higher in the with-description condition than in the without-description condition [22].

Hypothesis 5: Both measures of trust were expected to show lower trust in the false-alarm condition than in the miss condition [30], [31].

In addition to the above hypotheses, the current study also sought to explore how these factors interacted with each other in affecting user performance and trust in automation.

## III. METHODS

## A. Participants

A total of 510 participants (268 female, 241 male, 1 declined to say; age $M = 33.4, SD = 9.9$ were recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) and then directed to a Qualtrics website for the experiment. The MTurk population has been shown to be reasonably representative of the U.S. population in various domains, such as psychology and economics [36], [39], [40], and specifically in surveys about privacy and security [41]. On average, each participant spent approximately 15 min on the experiment and was paid \$1. To ensure the data quality, participants were screened based on their MTurk worker ID so that each ID could only sign up once. This article was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Old Dominion University.

## B. Apparatus, Stimuli, and Procedure

The experiment required participants to use a desktop or laptop computer to properly view the email images. Similar to [22], the stimuli were modified screenshots of 22 legitimate emails received by the authors, two of which served as practice; personal information was replaced with a fake user’s (Julia Smith) information. For each participant, half of the emails were crafted into phishing emails by altering the sender’s email address, and the other half remained unchanged and served as legitimate emails. This manipulation was used because the sender’s address has been shown to be the most reliable signifier of phishing emails [42]. These screenshots included a mixture of texts and images and fit on the screen so that participants could view each one without scrolling.

The study started with a question asking about participants knowledge of phishing (nothing, a bit, a lot), followed by a definition of phishing. At the start of the experiment, participants were instructed to review emails as if they were Julia. They were then shown emails in Julia’s email inbox, which they were to evaluate as legitimate or phishing. Next, they were given the definition of phishing emails as well as a description of a “phishingdetection system” that helps users identify phishing emails. For each email screenshot, participants first saw a recommendation by the phishing-detection system (phishing or legitimate). After seeing the recommendation, participants saw an email image and made their own decision about the email. After two practice trials that familiarized them with the task, each participant evaluated 20 emails in the experimental task. This number of 20 items was modeled after prior studies that used 20 items (e.g., websites or emails) to test users’ phishing-identification behaviors [7], [22], [42], [43]. Among the 20 emails, half were legitimate, and the other half were phishing emails. This 50% rate of phishing emails was determined to engage participants and reduce study costs [5]. The order of the emails was randomly determined for each participant. At the end of the experiment, participants answered questions regarding their demographic information and subjectively reported their trust in the phishing-detection system on a 7-point Likert scale (“I trusted the recommendations by the Phishing Detection System”; 1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree).

## C. Experimental Design

1) Independent Variables: There were four independent variables: reliability of the phishing-detection system (60% versus 90%), error type of the system (false-alarm versus miss), whether there was explicit description of the reliability (with versus without description), and whether feedback was provided after the participant’s decision (with versus without feedback). All independent variables were between-subjects, which resulted in 16 (2 reliability × 2 error type × 2 description × 2 feedback) distinct groups. Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the 16 groups, with 30 participants in each group. In addition, there was a separate control group of 30 participants with no automation aid.

To separate the effect of the error types of false alarms and misses, each participant only encountered one type of error. For each reliability level, half of the participants always encountered automation errors asfalse alarms, and the other half encountered all misses. In the false-alarm condition, the aid classified some of the legitimate emails as phishing; in the miss condition, the aid classified some of the phishing emails as legitimate. The number of emails with error recommendations from the aid was eight for the 60%-reliability group and two for the 90%-reliability group. These emails with error recommendations were randomly selected among the ten legitimate emails for each participant in the false-alarm condition and among the ten phishing emails for each participant in the miss condition.

Participants in the with-description groups were told the exact system reliability as “60%” or “90%,” and those in the withoutdescription groups were told that the system had a “reasonable” reliability. For example, the 60% with-description group was told “This Phishing Detection System is said to have a **60%** accurate rate,” and the 60% without-description group was told “This Phishing Detection System is said to have a **reasonable** accurate rate.” To ensure the validity of this description manipulation, the with-description group was then immediately tested on the stated percentage to make sure that they were fully aware of the reliability. The question asked was “What was the accurate rate for the Phishing Detection System, presented on the previous screen?” and participants were to select among options of 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90%, and 100%. Participants were reminded of the percentage if they did not answer it correctly. A total of 14 participants were reminded after the first attempt, all of whom answered correctly the second time.

As discussed earlier, we used feedback as the manipulation of experience. For the with-feedback groups, participants were provided feedback regarding their judgments after each email image. The feedback included whether the participant’s response was accurate and whether the previous email was phishing or legitimate. For the without-feedback groups, there was no feedback.

2) Dependent Variables: There were two categories of dependent variables, performance and trust. The performance measures included participants’ response sensitivity and criteria as in SDT [44] as well as decision time, and the trust measures included participants’ agreement rate with the phishing-detection system as an objective trust measure and self-reported trust in the system as a subjective trust measure.

SDT methods have been used in prior studies to examine users’ performance in phishing detection [5], [7], [42], [45], [46]. SDT characterizes how people respond to signals among noise, with the signals being phishing emails and noise being legitimate emails in the phishing context. Correctly identifying a phishing email counts as a hit and incorrectly identifying a legitimate email as phishing is classified as a false alarm. Based on the hit rates (H) and false-alarm rates (FA), measures of sensitivity (d’, reflecting the ability to distinguish phishing emails from legitimate emails) and response bias (c, tendency to report emails as phishing) are calculated. The measures in SDT provide a more complete picture of participants’ performance in classifying phishing and legitimate emails than a typical measure of judgment accuracy, and thus, we report these measures instead of overall accuracy. On the basis of classic SDT, a log-linear correction was applied to the calculations of H and FA to accommodate possible hit or false alarm rates of 0 or 1 [5], [46], [47]. Specifically, 0.5 was added to the numbers of hits and false alarms, and 1 was added to the number of signals and noise.

Decision time was measured starting from the time when an email was displayed to the time when the participant clicked the “Next” button to submit their decision. Decision time has been used in prior studies as a measure of user performance in identifying phishing emails [42]. The speed at which emails are classified is not only important to the user’s job and daily life but may also influence user experience and perception when the user interacts with automated systems [48], [49]. Accurate decisions with shorter decision times indicate better performance than those with longer decision times.

The agreement rate, or objective trust, was measured by how often the participant agreed with the aid’s recommendation out of the total 20 experimental emails. For example, when the aid determined the email to be legitimate and the participant classified the email as legitimate, then it was deemed that the participant agreed with the aid. This measure was not affected by how participants subjectively thought they trusted the aid. Subjectively reported trust was the answer that the participant marked on the 7-point Likert scale question to describe how much they thought that they trusted the recommendations by the phishing detection system at the end of the experiment.

## IV. RESULTS

A natural log transformation was conducted on the mean decision time of each participant to improve the normality of the data. The transformation, however, did not change the significance outcomes, and thus, we report the analyses without the transformation. Outlier data were determined based on the transformed decision time data, and 25 $(4.9\%)$ participants with mean decision times two standard deviations shorter or longer than the mean were excluded from subsequent analyses for all dependent variables. However, removing these observations did not change the significance results except for the main effect of error type on decision time (before removing outliers: M = 18.8 $\mathrm { s ,   S } D = 2 5 . 1$ s for the false-alarm conditions, $M = 15.8   s ,   SD$ $= 1 0 . 0 \mathrm { ~ s ~ }$ for the miss conditions, $F ( 1 ,   4 6 4 ) = 5 . 7 0 ,   p = . 0 1 7$ ${ \eta _ { p } } ^ { 2 } = . 0 1$ ; after removing outliers: $M = 16.0   s ,  SD = 7.9   s$ for the false-alarm conditions, $M = 15.4   s ,  SD = 7.9   s$ for the miss conditions, $F < 1 )$ .

Analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted with reliability, description, feedback, and error type as between-subjects factors on response sensitivity $( d ^ { \prime } )$ , response criterion (c), decision time, agreement rate, and self-reported trust, respectively, for the experimental groups. We followed the recommendations in [50] and conducted ANOVAs to examine the dependent variables that were conceptually separate. Rather than adjusting the alpha level, an alpha level of 0.05 was used to avoid an arbitrarily determined number of tests and increased chances of making type II errors [51]. Meanwhile, effect size was considered when determining the significance of effects reported below (i.e., the effect has to have at least a small effect size ${ \eta _ { p } } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 0 1$ to be significant).

That is, feedback reduced bias toward judging emails legitimate similarly at both reliability levels with false alarms: for the 60% reliability, $M = 0 . 0 9 , \mathit { S D } = 0 . 3 8$ with feedback, and $M = 0.27, SD = 0.71$ without feedback, $p = . 0 6 2 ;$ for the 90% reliability, $M = 0 . 0 5 , S D = 0 .$ 34 with feedback, and $M = 0 . 3 1 ,   S D = 0 . 5 9$ without feedback, $p = 0 . 0 0 9$

In summary, the effects of providing description and feedback on decision sensitivity depended on the reliability level–they were helpful at the 90% reliability level but not at the 60% level; the benefit of providing feedback on decision sensitivity was only evident when description was provided. Response bias was affected by the reliability level and feedback differently in the false-alarm and miss conditions. When the errors were false alarms, providing feedback reduced response bias toward judging emails as legitimate regardless of the reliability level; when the errors were misses, feedback was more helpful at the 60% reliability level than at the 90% level.

## B. Performance: Decision Time

The overall decision time across all experimental conditions was $15.7 \;  s  \; (SD = 7.9 \;  s )$ . The main effect of reliability was not significant $M = 16.0   s ,   SD = 7.7   s$ for the 60% reliability, $M = 15.4   s ,   SD = 8.0   s$ for the 90% reliability), $F < 1$ , not confirming the prediction on decision time in Hypothesis 1. A separate analysis showed that both conditions had longer decision times than the control condition $M = 11.0   s ,   SD =$ $3 . 7 \; \mathrm { s } ) , p \mathrm { s } = 0 . 0 1 2$ and 0.029, respectively. Providing feedback shortened the $\mathrm { d e c i s i o n ~ t i m e ~ } ( M = 1 5 . 0 ~ \mathrm { s } , S D = 8 . 2 ~ \mathrm { s }$ for withversus $M = 16.4    s ,   SD = 7.5    s$ for without-feedback conditions, respectively), $F(1,\;439)=3.83,\;p=0.050,\;\eta_{p}^{2}=0.01$ , in agreement with [22] and supporting the prediction of decision time in Hypothesis 2. The benefit of feedback was moderated by reliability and description. The reliability × feedback interaction was significant [see Fig. 3(a)], $F(1,439)=7.15,p=0.008,{\eta_{p}}^{2}$ $= 0 . 0 2$ The benefit of providing feedback was evident at the 90% reliability level $(M = 13.8   s ,   SD = 8.0   s$ with feedback versus $M = 17.1   s ,   SD = 7.8   s$ s without feedback, $p = 0 . 0 0 1 )$ , but not at the 60% level $(M = 16.3   s ,   SD = 8.3$ s with feedback versus $M = 15.7   s ,  SD = 7.2   s$ without feedback), $p = 0 . 6 1 2$ The description × feedback interaction was also significant [see Fig. 3(b)], $F(1,439)=4.63,p=0.032,{\eta_{p}}^{2}=0.01$ . The benefit of feedback was evident when the description was also present $M = 14.23   s ,   SD = 8.4   s$ with feedback versus $M = 1 7 . 3$ s , $S D = 7 . 5 ~ \mathrm { s }$ without feedback), $p = 0 . 0 0 4$ , but not when it was absent $( M = 1 5 . 8 \; \mathrm { s } , S D = 8 . 0$ s with feedback versus $M = 1 5 . 6$ $s , S D = 7 . 5 \; \mathrm { s }$ without feedback), $p = 0 . 8 8 9$ . No effect involving error type was significant, $F \mathrm { s } < 1 . 4 8 .$

## C. Trust: Agreement Rate

The mean agreement rate across all experimental conditions was $63.2\% \left(SD = 18.7\%\right)$ . Participants’ agreement rate with the phishing-detection system differed across the two error types (M $=  57.3\%,   SD  =  20.1\%$ for false-alarm conditions versus M = $69.2\%, SD = 15.0\%$ for miss conditions), $F ( 1 , 4 3 9 ) = 6 5 . 2 2 , p$ $< 0.001,{\eta_{p}}^{2} = 0.13$ , supporting the prediction of objective trust in Hypothesis 5. The agreement rate was higher with the 90% system $(M = 69.1\%, SD = 15.7\%)$ than with the 60% system (M $= 57.4\%,  SD  = 19.6\%), F(1, 439) = 63.85, p < 0.001, {\eta_{p}}^{2} =$ 0.13, supporting the prediction of objective trust in Hypothesis 1. Providing feedback also increased the agreement rate $( M =$ 61.6%, $SD = 20.2\%$ with feedback versus $M = 64.9\%,   SD =$ 17.0% without feedback), $F(1,439)=4.78,p=0.029,{\eta_{p}}^{2}=$ 0.01, supporting the prediction of objective trust in Hypothesis 2.

All the two-way interactions among reliability, feedback, and error type were significant (see Fig. 4). There was a significant reliability × feedback interaction, $F(1,439)=31.82,p<0.001$ ${ \eta _ { p } } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 0 7$ . The agreement rate was higher with feedback (M $=  74.8\%,   SD  =  14.5\%)$ than without feedback $(M = 63.4\%)$ $SD = 14.7\%$ at the 90% reliability level, $p < 0 . 0 0 1$ . However, it showed an opposite effect at the 60% level $(M = 54.9\%)$

In summary, when the errors were misses, participants trusted the unreliable system less and trusted the reliable system more with feedback than without feedback; when the errors were false alarms, participants trusted the reliable system more with feedback than without feedback but distrusted the unreliable system equally with or without feedback. Thus, it is fair to conclude that providing feedback helped calibrate objective trust in both the miss and false-alarm conditions.

## D. Trust: Self-Reported Trust

The overall self-reported trust across all experimental conditions was 4.3 $( S D = 1 . 5 )$ , with 4 being neutral. The agreement rate and self-reported trust were significantly correlated, Pearson’s $r = 0 . 4 4 ,   n = 4 5 5 ,   p < 0 . 0 0 1$ . Similar to the agreement rate, higher trust was reported with increased reliability $( M =$ $3 . 9 , S D = 1 . 6 ,$ vs. M = 4.6, SD = 1.4 for reliability levels of 60% and 90%, respectively), $F(1, 439) = 30.31,   p < 0.001,   {\eta_{p}}^{2} =$ $0 . 0 7$ , supporting the prediction of subjective trust in Hypothesis 1. Feedback did not show a significant main effect, $F   <   1$ , against the prediction of subjective trust in Hypothesis 2. Misses only showed numerically higher trust than false alarms $( M = 4 . 4 ,$ $S D = 1 . 5$ versus $M = 4 . 1 ,   S D = 1 . 6 )$ , but this effect did not attain the 0.05 significance level or the effect size criterion of $0.01,   F(1,   439)   =   2.98,   p   =   0.085,   \eta_{p}   =   0.007$ , failing to support the prediction of subjective trust in Hypothesis 5. No term involving description was significant and thus failed to support the prediction of subjective trust in Hypothesis 4.

The reliability × feedback interaction was significant [see Fig. 6(a)], $F(1,\;439)=5.24,\;p=0.023,\;\eta_{p}^{2}=0.01$ . With feedback, participants reported higher trust in the 90% system $(M = 4.8, SD = 1.4)$ than in the 60% system $(M = 3.7, SD = 1.5)$ $p   <   0 . 0 0 1$ ; without feedback, they still trusted the 90% system (M $4.5, SD = 1.3$ more than the 60% system $( M = 4.0, SD = 1.7 )$ $p = 0 . 0 2 4$ , thus partially supporting the prediction of subjective trust in Hypothesis 3. The feedback × error type interaction was also significant [see $Fig. 6(b)],F(1,439)=4.35,p=0.038,\eta_{p}^{2}$ $= 0 . 0 1$ . Lower trust was reported in the false-alarm condition $( M = 4 . 0 ,   S D = 1 . 6 )$ than in the miss condition $( M = 4 . 5 ,   S D$ $= 1 . 4 )$ without feedback, $p = 0 . 0 0 8$ ; the difference between the two error types was not significant with feedback $( M = 4 . 3 , S D$ $= 1 . 5$ for false alarms, $M = 4.3, \; SD = 1.5$ for misses), $p   =   0 . 7 9 8 .$ The overall reliability percentage was the same regardless of the error type. Thus, it seems that providing feedback increased trust calibration not only by lowering trust in the unreliable system and increasing trust in the reliable system but also by eliminating the difference in trust between the two error types.

In summary, the results of subjective trust showed similar patterns to those of the objective agreement rate, although the subjective measure was not as sensitive as the objective measure. The trust-calibration function of feedback on subjective trust was evident only in the miss conditions, in which providing feedback increased trust at the 90% reliability level and reduced trust at the 60% reliability level.

## V. DISCUSSION

The effectiveness of communicating the system capabilities to the user is critical for the user’s trust in the automated system [11]. The two ways of communicating system capabilities of interest include an explicit description of system capabilities and users experiencing the system with feedback. Moreover, automated systems are imperfect and make errors resulting in false alarms or misses. These different types of errors also affect users’ trust in and interaction with automated systems, even given the same overall system reliability [52]. In the present study, participants made decisions on legitimate or phishing emails with assistance from a phishing-detection system. We examined how the automation error type and the methods of communicating the system reliability information affected users’ trust and performance in both reliable (90% reliability) and unreliable (60% reliability) systems.

## A. Performance

In terms of performance, when the system reliability increased from 60% to 90%, participants’ decision sensitivity was improved, indicating that the phishing-detection system, even though simulated, was utilized in the participants’ decision process. This result is in line with prior research showing that automated systems with higher reliability improve performance [22], [30], [31], [52]. Importantly, providing feedback on the participant’s decision resulted in increased decision sensitivity and shortened decision time, although only for reliable systems. Feedback also alleviated the response bias toward judging emails as legitimate for all groups. Providing an explicit description of system reliability also exerted effects on performance: the description of system reliability increased decision sensitivity at the 90% reliability level, increased decision sensitivity, and reduced decision time when feedback was also provided. Al though providing description and feedback is a choice of the designer and manufacturer, our results demonstrated the benefits of keeping users informed of both system capabilities and their decision outcomes.

During the experiment, feedback was provided regarding participants’ own decisions, which was expected to have a positive effect on participants’ performance [37], [38]. However, the benefit of feedback in the current study was compromised when the unreliable system was used as an aid. These results indicate that the aid being reliable is the premise of it being useful to users. With a reliable system, providing feedback and description increased response sensitivity. The design implication is that designers should include both description and feedback in the interface of an automation aid whenever possible, provided that the aid is reliable.

Overall, participants’ performance in classifying the phishing and legitimate emails was poor in the experiment $( d ^ { \prime } = 0 . 3 8$ with the 60%-reliability aid and 0.89 with the 90%-reliability aid, with 0 being at the chance level and 3.38 close to perfect). This poor performance corresponded to the low subjective trust and agreement rate at the 60% reliability level (3.9, 57.3%) and the 90% level (4.6, 69.2%). A possible reason is that we used a difficult task [22]. The only feature that distinguished the phishing emails from the legitimate emails was the sender’s email address. The sender’s address has been shown to be the most effective signifier in determining phishing emails [42], and training tools have focused on teaching users about this signifier [7]. However, our data showed that users were poor at identifying phishing emails based on the sender’s address. Participants may have strongly believed in their own decisions when identifying the phishing emails as legitimate. As a result, when the aid classified the emails as phishing, their trust in the aid degraded. Note that the phishing-detection system in the current study did not provide any transparency information regarding how the recommendations were made. Transparency has been shown to increase users’ trust in automated systems (see [12] for a review). This lack of transparency could have also contributed to the low trust level in the current study.

## B. Trust Measures

The objective trust measure (agreement rate) and the subjective trust measure (self-reported trust) showed similar results patterns, although the subjective trust measure was less sensitive. Thus, we discuss the general result pattern in terms of trust rather than separating these two measures. Across the two error types, the overall trust level was higher when the errors were misses than when they were false alarms, in line with prior studies that showed false alarms lower human trust in automation more than misses do [31]. This result may be because misses are more likely to be unnoticed than false alarms. With misses, participants trusted the system more without noticing the errors; with false alarms, participants were constantly reminded by the errors that the system was not capable of making correct decisions.

More importantly, our results also showed that the cost of trust due to false alarms was influenced to different degrees for unreliable and reliable systems. The cost of false alarms was greater for the unreliable system, which counterintuitively was a benefit—people trusted the unreliable system too much with misses but calibrated their trust in the unreliable system to be appropriately lower with false alarms. In other words, it was problematic when participants were working with an aid that was unreliable and made all miss errors. When the aid was reliable, the system made fewer errors, and participants trusted the system more regardless of the error type; this led to properly calibrated trust because participants were expected to trust the reliable system. When the aid was unreliable, false alarms were noticeably frequent so that trust was lower; this also led to properly calibrated trust because participants were expected not to trust the unreliable system. However, when the system was unreliable and the errors were all misses, participants would not notice the misses enough to lower their trust in the system, leading to an inappropriate level of trust calibration. Thus, a design implication from our finding is that for systems that are unreliable, misses are less desirable than false alarms.

## C. Trust Calibration

It is noteworthy that feedback helped with trust calibration, demonstrated by the interactions between feedback and reliability level in both the false-alarm and miss conditions. Calibrated trust (i.e., trust matches system capabilities) is essential for effective human–automation interaction [11]. Our results showed that when feedback was provided, participants trusted the automation aid less when it was unreliable and more when it was reliable, confirming the findings in [22]. The possible reason for this result pattern is that when feedback was provided, participants were able to compare recommendations of the system with the feedback. This comparison made it evident to the participants whether the system was reliable or not, regardless of the description.

Moreover, it is interesting that the trust-calibration function of feedback was mostly evident for both the false-alarm and miss conditions. As mentioned, false alarms decreased trust more than misses, which was counterintuitively helpful for unreliable systems. However, the decrease in trust caused by false alarms for reliable systems, although not as much as that for unreliable systems, was still troublesome because appropriate calibration requires higher trust for more reliable systems. Feedback helped calibrate trust to a higher level in this case. These results again indicate the importance of including feedback, considering not only performance but also trust.

In the real world, users may receive limited feedback regarding the consequences of phishing [5], [22], although the feedback may not be as immediate and clear as that used in the current study. However, there are still ways for users to potentially receive feedback. For example, if a user entered information onto a phishing website, a bank could immediately give them a notification that nefarious activity was detected on their account, showing that they might have been a part of a phishing scam. In addition, every time users respond to an email and obtain a subsequent response back from that recipient, this is a type of feedback and experience that the email was from a legitimate entity and was not phishing. As phishing-detection aids improve in the future, they could also issue feedback to users based on other users’ actions. For instance, if many users received similar emails and many marked them as phishing, the system could retroactively notify the user that the email they ignored or reported was treated as phishing by others.

## D. Limitations

One limitation of the study was that there were equal numbers of phishing and legitimate emails (i.e., 50% target prevalence). In the real world, however, most emails that a common user receives are legitimate emails [53], [54]. It was shown that the base rate of target signals affected the errors participants made in a visual search task [55]. The larger number of legitimate emails than that of phishing emails potentially makes false alarms more likely than misses in the real world. On the one hand, it is likely that false alarms may annoy users and be ignored by the users [56], [57]; on the other hand, misses may annoy users when consequences of getting phished become evident [58]. Moreover, our participants were asked to imagine themselves as Julia Smith and deal with emails with this name. The emails, as well as the potential consequences, were not as personally related to the participants as in the real world. Further research would be valuable to examine whether the results of this study generalize to more realistic target-prevalence conditions and to simulate real-world consequences of both error types and study the effect of user annoyance on antiphishing aids.

Another limitation was introduced by the isolation of the error types in this article. The participants experienced an automated aid with all misses or all false alarms, whereas in the real world, there could be a mix of them. For this experiment, to examine the influence of the two error types individually, it was necessary to separate them. However, as mentioned in Section I, there is usually a tradeoff between false alarms and misses, and they are not all or none. With a mixture of misses and false alarms, the trust-calibration process may have been affected differently. As a result, future studies may test how the proportions of false alarms and misses affect the human operator’s trust-calibration process toward the system.

In addition, it is likely that participants’ performance and trust in the antiphishing aid may change over time. Participants in this article classified 20 emails following two practice trials, and it could have taken time for them to learn about the system, especially for those in the no-description conditions who were told that the reliability was “reasonable.” We were not able to analyze how their data changed over time due to a programming limitation on recording the order of the emails presented to them. Future studies should include a familiarization phase to ensure that participants have sufficiently understood the system before collecting their data; alternatively, future studies can investigate how interacting with the antiphishing aid affects users’ performance and trust dynamically and validate various trust measures over time.

Last, users’ prior experience of using antiphishing aids and their personal characteristics, such as personality and Internet self-efficacy, may influence their decisions on phishing emails [59]. This influence is beyond the scope of this article. However, future studies can further examine how these factors interact with the reliability and error type of aid and affect users’ decisions and trust in automated aid.

## VI. CONCLUSION

This article investigated how human trust and performance, when interacting with an automated aid, were affected by the methods of communicating the automation reliability information as well as the types of automation errors. The results showed that learning the automation reliability information through immediate feedback improved participants’ performance and helped calibrate trust in accordance with the system reliability. Informing participants about the exact reliability level of the system improved performance to some extent when the aid was reliable but did not have much effect on trust. Moreover, false alarms lowered trust more than did misses, although this lower trust turned out to be beneficial when the aid was unreliable.
